title: Every other door
hookLine: leaving every other door, I have come to Yours; keep my honor (Chaupai, dohra)

lines: ALL THE DOORS YOU'VE KNOCKED ON.
cards: Count the doors you've knocked on in your life. The literal ones: job interviews, the landlord, the new neighbor.
And the other kind: the friend you hoped would understand, the qualification that would make you enough, the achievement that was going to fix everything. Some opened. Some didn't.
Some opened onto rooms that turned out to be empty. Chaupai ends with someone at the end of that list, having tried them all, standing now at one last door.

teach.b: The closing couplet, a dohra, goes like this in paraphrase: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of your door. You who have taken my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant.
Duaar means door. Sagal duaar, every door. Tuhaaro duaar, your door.
And there's the picture from day three hundred seventy-one: baanh gahe, the one who has taken my arm. In Punjabi, to take someone's arm is a promise of protection, the kind you don't walk away from.

teach.h: YOU WHO TOOK MY ARM, KEEP MY HONOR.
teach.b: So the couplet says: you made a promise when you took my arm; keep it, keep my honor. Laaj, the word for honor here, is close to dignity and good name. It's a very human thing to ask: don't let me be shamed.

Gobind is your servant. Guru Gobind Singh signs the last line of his prayer not as Guru, not as leader of the Khalsa, but as Gobind das, the servant: the same humility as yesterday's I have not said this.

teach.h: FROM A HAND TO AN ARM, TO A DOOR.
teach.b: The prayer began with a hand and ends with an arm, taken.
The heart's wish was to stay at the feet; it ends at the door, having left every other. A whole prayer, one movement: a person walking past every other option to the one place they want to be kept.
Some Sikhs say this couplet on its own in moments of fear, as if it carried the whole Chaupai in two lines.

how: Many Sikhs recite this closing dohra as part of Chaupai Sahib and Rehras, and some say it on its own in moments of fear as a short prayer for protection.

o: a wall that keeps strangers out
a door, the one you choose to stand at
the road that leads a pilgrim home

games.q: every other door — tap the pairs.
p: the one who has taken my arm

s: Guru Gobind Singh signs the last line as the Lord's servant
Gobind das tuhaar: Gobind is your servant.
the couplet asks the Lord to open every door
it leaves every other door and holds on to one: your door.
the prayer's opening and closing pictures are unrelated
it begins with a hand and ends with an arm taken: one movement from start to finish.

games.q: you've knocked on every door there is: wealth, praise, power, people. you're at the last one. what does Chaupai's couplet say?
o: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of yours; keep my honor.
games.why: sagal duaar kau chhaad kai gahio tuhaaro duaar: leaving every door, I hold yours. and then, Gobind is your servant.

practice: If you can, stand in an open doorway at home, right in the frame, and feel the threshold under your feet: one room behind you, another ahead.

Think of the doors you've knocked on, the ones that opened and the ones that didn't, and let them go, one by one. If you pray, say Waheguru, standing at this door; if not, notice how it feels to stop knocking and simply stand.

wordCard.voice: Duaar, door. Chaupai's last couplet: leaving every other door I have come to yours; you who took my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: duaar, door; in Chaupai's last couplet, every other door left behind for one.

carryVoice: Your line: your door. One last door, and an arm already taken. Day three hundred seventy-eight, done.
